Stand-alone edition (V1): no, ever. V1 makes no network calls at all and has no account layer. If you want Cockpit with no registration, this is the edition to install — it is the same download, you just choose Stand-alone when the installer asks.

Once past that, the account layer itself is still only about the online/shared-content side: marketplace, subscriptions, credits. Your local features — agents, models, tools, media, projects — neither check it nor report to it.

If the account panel appears on an install that was signed in, it means the server could not confirm this machine. Sign in again; if the network is simply down, a previously validated licence keeps working offline. One exception, in the Full edition: Autopilot Cruise and AutoCognition pause while Cockpit cannot reach the account server (the last check failed, or the last good answer is over a week old). They come back by themselves at the next successful check, which runs every ten minutes. Everything else keeps working.

Update — September 2026: New features

Everything below is in the current build. The short version: Cockpit reads more kinds of material (books, PDF pages, images, audio), tells you where an answer came from, and can be driven without the keyboard.

Margin — write in the margin of a file

Select a few lines in the Files viewer, say what should change, and the agent answers with the replacement for exactly those lines. Nothing is written until you have seen the diff and pressed Apply.

The agent never edits the file. It produces text; Cockpit does the splice, against the file as it is on disk at that moment, and only after you agree. The anchor travels with the request — file, line range, and the exact text selected — so the agent is not asked to find the place again and cannot drift onto a similar-looking passage further down. And only the replacement is requested: asking a model to re-emit a whole file to change three lines invites silent losses in the parts nobody reviews.

Apply checks first. It re-reads the file and looks for your selected lines again. If they have changed since you asked, or now appear in more than one place, it refuses with those lines no longer match the file and writes nothing — an edit elsewhere in the file is fine, because the lines are found again wherever they now are. After a successful Apply the open preview re-reads the file, so you see the change at once; the viewer’s header also has a refresh button that re-reads the file from disk whenever it has been changed by something else.

Dossier — a researched answer with sources you can check

Ask a question. Cockpit searches several framings of it, reads the pages, and hands the agent a numbered source pack with one instruction: answer from these and cite them. The report is saved into the project as Markdown, so it lands in Artifacts with everything else the project produced.

The gathering is deterministic: the same question fetches the same pages whichever agent writes the report, so a small local model can do the writing without having to drive a search loop it would get lost in.

Status. Dossier’s first step is a web search, and public search engines increasingly refuse automated queries — on some networks every one answers with a bot check, and Dossier comes back empty. It is paused until it can draw on sources that do not depend on them.

The honest limit, which the report states about itself: this reads the first pages a search engine returns. It is a fast survey, not a literature review — and the sources are listed precisely so you can judge them yourself.

Profile — what every agent should know about you

Directives say how agents should behave. Profile says who they are working with: units, language, timezone, how you like answers, what you are building.

It rides on every prompt, which is why the editor shows its size and caps it — a profile that grows into an essay quietly taxes every request and crowds out the actual question. Two ways in: the editor, or Remember this on any message, which appends a single line (it refuses duplicates).

The first time you open it, you see a sample that says plainly that it is one. Nothing is saved until you save, and no agent has seen it: the sample is never written to disk, because anything on disk is put in front of every agent.

Intercom — talk to the rig, hands free

Press once: Cockpit listens, notices when you stop talking, transcribes what you said, sends it, speaks the answer, and listens again. Press again to stop.

Two behaviours worth knowing:

  • Silence ends your turn, not a timer. The turn closes about 1.5 seconds after you stop speaking, because a fixed window either cuts people off or makes them wait. A minimum length stops a cough being sent as a prompt.
  • It speaks the answer, not the markup. Code blocks, tables and marker syntax are stripped before the text reaches the voice, and long answers are cut with a spoken note rather than read aloud for four minutes.

Bookshelf — a book the agent can actually use

Press the Bookshelf button in the Toolbar, pick a book with Browse… (epub, docx, odt, fb2 via pandoc; mobi and friends via calibre) and Cockpit splits it into chapters and files them in the Library, where it appears as a single foldable row. Conversion markup left over from the book’s source is stripped when the text is read, so books filed earlier read cleanly too.

Converting was never the hard part — scale was. Over ~50 KB of extracted text an agent only gets a file path and a preview, which is fine for an agent with file tools and useless for a local model. Because chapters are filed individually, retrieval pulls only the chapter that matches your question and Receipts names it, so a 400-page book works with a 7B model: it never sees more than the chapter it needs.

Books can live anywhere. Browse… in the native window opens the system file chooser and uses the real path; in a plain browser the file dialog hands the bytes over and Cockpit keeps a copy in your data folder; or type a path. A typed path must be inside a folder Cockpit may read (your projects and data folders); if it is not, the message names them and offers Allow <folder>, which records that folder as approved. Cockpit never reads a folder you have not approved, and it never copies in a file on your behalf from a path you typed. Browse remembers the last folder you used.

Chapters are sized to your machine. Each chapter is cut to about 12, 20 or 40 KB depending on the video memory Cockpit detects, because a chapter too large for a small card made prompt processing take minutes. A book whose headings are marked in a way Cockpit does not recognise falls back to numbered parts (Part 1, Part 2, …).

The chapter list is shown before anything is written, because a bad split (a book with no headings, a PDF that extracts as one blob) is obvious in a preview and invisible afterwards.

PDF Vision — the pages, not just the text

Attaching a PDF extracts its text (with pdftotext) and puts it in your prompt. But text extraction loses whatever was never text: diagrams, scans, tables that were drawn rather than typed, handwriting — a scanned book has no text at all.

Turn on the PDF Vision capability (Capabilities tab; it is off by default because rendering pages costs time) and Cockpit also renders the first six pages as images and hands them to an agent that can see, so a page is read as a page. Claude opens the page images itself; other agents receive them the way their catalog entry says, or a local description of the first three pages.

Ask your question in the same message as the attachment. The page images belong to that one message; a question sent afterwards no longer has them.

Vision dispatch — each agent gets the image the way it can take one

Attached images are no longer handled one single way. Each supplier entry in the agent catalog declares how it accepts an image, and Cockpit dispatches accordingly — one agent is given the file path to open itself, another takes an explicit image flag. Where an agent genuinely cannot see, Cockpit says so and falls back to a description rather than pretending: a CLI that silently invents a description of an image it never received is worse than an error.

The describe locally route needs a local vision model (ollama pull gemma3:4b). If it is not installed, Cockpit tells you in the chat that this agent cannot see the picture and how to fix that, and tells the agent in plain words not to describe or guess it. (A small model given only a file path will otherwise invent a picture — the same file once came back as a blue circle and a red square, then as a red circle, a blue square and a green triangle.) The agent editor’s Can it see? test says could not run here when the agent is not signed in or has no key in the test, rather than blaming its eyes: for those, test from a chat on a card.

Privacy and spending — what may leave this computer

The Privacy button in the Toolbar holds three rules. They run before a prompt is queued for an agent, so a refused prompt leaves nothing behind.

Sensitivity gate. A prompt headed for an online agent is checked for private keys, API keys and tokens, passwords in assignments, passwords inside connection strings, and payment-card, IBAN and US social-security numbers that pass their own checksum. If something is found, nothing is sent until you choose Redact and send (each item is replaced by [REDACTED:type] and the chat says what was removed), Use the local model instead, Send anyway, or Cancel. In Privacy & spending you can instead choose a standing rule: Ask me every time (the default), Never send them online, unless I choose to, each time (the safe choices come first and Send anyway needs a second, explicit confirmation), Redact automatically and tell me, or Never send them online, no exceptions. It is deliberately conservative: there is no rule for names, e-mail addresses or phone numbers, and obvious placeholders (your_api_key, ${TOKEN}, xxxx) are ignored, because a gate that cries wolf gets switched off. Local agents are never checked, since nothing leaves the machine; Workers are checked the same way as the cards. Nothing found is stored: only the type and the first four characters are ever shown.

Free agents only. Refuses agents that need a paid plan, with a plain message. It is linked with Stay Free in the Suppliers dialog: Stay Free is the one-time action that picks free agents for the cards, and Free agents only is the standing rule that refuses paid ones at send time. Pressing Stay Free also turns the rule on and tells you so; while the rule is on, the Suppliers dialog shows a banner, disables the paid agents (“paid, blocked”) and warns if a card still holds one. If you want the two to work independently, untick Link with Stay Free in the Suppliers dialog in Privacy & spending. “Paid” means the same in both places: an agent that needs a paid plan and is not flagged free in the agent catalog. It is on by default for a new install and off for an install that already has history, so an update never starts refusing the agent you have been using.

Monthly budget. A limit on prompts to paid agents per calendar month (0 means no limit). Cockpit cannot see what a subscription bills, so it counts what it can measure. It warns at 80%, stops at 100%, and lets you send one prompt anyway.

The Try the gate box is a dry run: paste any text, press Check, and it lists what the gate would catch (the kind of item and its first four characters) and shows the text as it would be sent after redaction. Use it to see what the gate understands before you rely on it, or to check a snippet you are unsure about. It runs on this machine’s own rules; nothing pasted there is stored or sent anywhere.

Auto Generate: palette types and picked colours

+ New in the Theme Editor opens the new-theme panel; Auto Generate makes a random theme of the chosen mode. The row For Auto Generate shapes it:

  • Palette: Normal (a random hue, the agents spread round the colour wheel); High contrast (near-black or near-white surfaces, pure text, saturated bright agent colours); Protanopia, Deuteranopia, Tritanopia (colours that stay apart for red-, green- or blue-weak or -blind eyes; the milder forms, protanomaly, deuteranomaly and tritanomaly, are covered by the same sets); Achromatopsia (no colour at all: greys, the six agents told apart by lightness).

It is an aid, not a medical guarantee, and the agent names are always shown as well.
  • Plates, not gradients. Readability guard for every theme

Whenever a theme is applied – built-in, one you made, edited or imported – Cockpit checks each text colour against the surfaces it sits on and repairs any that cannot be read, in the applied copy (your saved theme is not rewritten):

  • Agent and accent colours (agent names, clock, supplier labels, active buttons) 3.3:1 on the content surfaces.

Also fixed in the same change: in the nine Mixed themes the Theme Editor’s own drop-downs showed dark text on a dark background, and the project-kind picker could open with an empty list if the first request was made before you were signed in. ## Very long answers no longer empty a chat {#long-answers}

Until build 189, an agent answer of about 128 KB or more (a large generated file, a long document) made the step that saves the turn fail, and that step then replaced the whole chat file with an empty one: every earlier turn of that chat was lost and the answer was not saved either. This is fixed: the turn goes into the chat file through a temporary file, and the chat file is left untouched if saving fails. Nothing to configure.

The native agent runtime (optional, off by default)

Cockpit’s agent loop is a long Bash script. Three of its jobs now also exist as small native programs that do the same thing without jq, awk, sed, sqlite3 or python3: starting the agent’s command line (aicengine, written in Free Pascal and installed beside the scripts), choosing and rendering the earlier turns of a chat (history_cli.php), and carrying out the %%CREATE%%, %%READ%% and similar commands in a reply (crud_cli.php). Each was checked against the Bash it replaces on the same inputs: more than 290 comparisons, including your own chat files.

They are off. To try them, create an empty file called use_engine in your Cockpit data folder (~/scripts/cockpit_data/use_engine), or start the loop with COCKPIT_ENGINE=1. Delete the file to go back. If the engine is missing or refuses a request, the loop uses its Bash exactly as before.

The engine also makes the Gemini call (card 2 when it points at Google’s API): it speaks HTTPS itself and checks the server’s certificate and host name every time; a certificate that is not trusted, or is for another name, is refused and nothing is sent. The API key goes in a request header, not in the web address, and never appears on a command line. A prompt of any size goes through (the Bash path stopped working around 128 KB). A failed connection now says why instead of ending with an empty error line. In both paths a Gemini reply that holds no text (a safety block, an empty candidate) now shows the reason (“[GEMINI ERROR] SAFETY”) instead of a blank answer.

The engine also assembles the prompt for each turn (the project’s goal, kind and descriptions, COCKPIT.md, your profile, the global directives, the identity line and the layout for the agent), without jq and about twice as fast. It was proven identical to the shell version on 156 cases, including the awkward ones (a goal cut mid-character, COCKPIT.md at exactly 8 KB, broken JSON files). One shell habit is gone with it: a prompt that is exactly -n or -e is no longer swallowed as an option.

The engine also does the clean-up after the agent answers: it strips terminal artifacts from an Ollama or Gemini reply (carriage returns, colour codes, Ollama’s progress line, the Gemini CLI’s colour warnings and fallback notices), times the turn, writes the Ollama usage line, and adds the “installed but not signed in” hint to a short reply that says so. It was proven identical to the shell version on 304 cases. Two shell weaknesses are gone with it: it needs no sed, bc or GNU date (on macOS the shell version could not even time a turn), and the Ollama usage line is valid JSON whatever the chat is called (a backslash in a chat name used to make that line unreadable for the Usage page).

The engine also does the start of every turn: it finds the request’s details (project, chat, models, per-user folders), the Ollama model file and the supplier controls, puts the effort text in front of the prompt, keeps the extra command-line arguments only when they pass the safety whitelist, and removes the queue files. It was proven identical to the shell version on 56 cases (including pretty-printed and CRLF request files, escaped slashes, awkward base64 and an empty or -n prompt), and by running the whole loop twice with a stand-in agent. When a control is not clean base64, the engine steps aside before touching anything and the shell version does the turn.

What changes when it is on: a faster history step (about 35 ms instead of 60, and a new chat’s first call 20 ms instead of 220); the agent’s standard input is closed so an agent that waits for input cannot look stuck; pressing Stop ends the agent and everything it started; and %%DELETE:.%% can no longer delete a whole project folder. One cosmetic difference: some agents (Aider, for one) print a note that their input is not a terminal.

Markers that call Cockpit’s own pages now work. When an agent writes %%FETCH:url%%, %%SEARCH:terms%%, %%WORKER:...%%, %%TOOL:...%% or %%PROPOSE:...%%, the agent loop asks search.php, workers.php, tools.php or library.php on this machine. Those requests carried no login, so every one was answered “Authentication required” and the markers silently did nothing (the Workers and Tools lists the loop offers the agent were empty for the same reason). The loop now keeps a small secret in the data folder (internal_key, readable only by you and the web server’s group, created by the loop, never by a web page) and sends it with the name of the person the request belongs to. The pages accept it only when the request comes from this machine without passing through a proxy, names one of exactly these page-and-action pairs (search/fetch, models/invoke, presets/run, proposal_add), and names a person who exists, with the role that person has (a viewer stays a viewer). Everything else on the site still needs a login. A second bug lay behind the first: %%PROPOSE%% used names library.php did not know, so a proposal would have failed even with a login; it now works. A V1 loop also used to call V2’s pages; it now calls its own edition’s.

The whole agent loop as a native program (optional, off by default)

With a file called use_native_loop in the Cockpit data folder (or use_native_loop_ollama, use_native_loop_claude, use_native_loop_gemini for one agent only), each agent’s queue loop runs as one native program (aicengine loop) instead of the shell script: it finds the request, works out which supplier the card means, applies the project’s capabilities and auto-route lists, assembles the prompt, runs the agent, cleans the answer, carries out the %%markers%%, saves the exchange and signals that it is done. It needs none of jq, sed, bc, python3 or curl. PHP is still used for two things, as before: the chat history and saving the turn (history_cli.php) and the markers (crud_cli.php). Without PHP there is no history, and the turn is saved by the program itself.

It was proven against the shell loop by running both on the same thirteen requests (a stand-in Claude, a catalog CLI on card 1 and on card 2, a mock Ollama, a marker that creates a file, effort text and arguments, the not-signed-in hint, a request with no details file, and follow-ups with earlier turns in the chat): the answer, a hash of the whole prompt, the saved chat, the files created and the log lines are identical. The old script is not removed: delete use_native_loop and restart the agents to go back. tmux and the supervisor start the same command as before, which hands over to the native program.

Also in this build: the capabilities and auto-route steps of the shell loop can run in the engine too (69 cases proven identical), and the engine’s loop keeps one loop per agent through the same pid file.

The native loop also does the chat history itself: deciding whether a prompt needs the earlier turns, picking the relevant ones from the chat’s search index, and saving each turn into the chat file. It uses the same index file as before (SQLite, loaded from the system’s library when it is there; without it the loop sends the last turns instead, as the shell version does) and needs no PHP for this. It was proven identical to the PHP helper on 1,743 cases. For the few inputs it does not copy exactly (text that is not valid UTF-8, an unusual character, a chat file written by a very old version), it hands that one request to the PHP helper if there is one.

The markers an agent writes (%%CREATE%%, %%APPEND%%, %%READ%%, %%DELETE%%, %%MKDIR%%, %%LIST%%, %%FETCH%%, %%SEARCH%%, %%WORKER%%, %%TOOL%%, %%PROPOSE%% and the library markers) are carried out by the engine as well, in the same process, with the same one-line results the agent has always been shown (148 checks against the shell executor and the PHP helper, including the requests sent to Cockpit’s own pages). It sends the loop’s private key only to those pages, never to a catalog entry’s address. A few worker or tool answers it will not format itself (numbers with decimals, lists, objects); for those the PHP helper does that one marker. With the native loop on, a machine without PHP runs chat, history and markers entirely natively; the shell loop’s marker step uses the engine too when the engine switch is on.

The free-REST suppliers of card 2 (Groq, HuggingFace, Cloudflare) are called by the engine too: it opens your encrypted Workers key store (the same AES-256-GCM file, the same machine-bound key) and makes the one request the PHP relay would make, with the same answer and the same error texts (46 checks against worker_relay.php, including the request each side sends). It hands the job to the PHP relay for what it will not reproduce exactly: another provider, a store it cannot read, a redirect, an answer of an unusual shape. The one visible difference: when the provider cannot be reached at all, the message reads “curl:” followed by this program’s own reason. With the native loop on, no PHP is needed for card 2 either.

The web front is a second, optional way to serve Cockpit. With a file called use_aicserver in the Cockpit data folder (put a port number in it to choose the port; otherwise 8081 for the full edition and 8082 for the stand-alone one), the supervisor also runs aicserver (a small Free Pascal web server) and php-cgi as you, and Cockpit answers on http://127.0.0.1:8081/cockpit/ as well as on Apache’s port. Apache is untouched and stays the default; this is for trying the replacement and for machines without Apache. It needs php-cgi (sudo apt install php8.3-cgi) and the supervisor switched on. It refuses the same files Apache refuses (your settings, usage log, quota file, the queue and response folders). Remove the file to stop using it.

Starting Cockpit without Apache. The menu has a second entry, AI Cockpit (self-contained) (and AI Cockpit V1 (self-contained)), and the terminal commands cockpit-self-start and cockpit-v1-self-start. They do what the ordinary start does (agents, splash, the same native window) but serve the app from aicserver instead of Apache: the supervisor runs the web server and PHP as you, the window opens on http://127.0.0.1:8081/cockpit/ (V1: port 8082), and Apache is not started. The first time, it creates the two switch files for you (use_supervisor and use_aicserver in that edition’s data folder); after that the web server simply stays part of the supervisor, so both ways of starting work side by side. It needs aicserver, php-cgi and the supervisor; if one is missing it says so and opens the Apache address instead. Both editions work: V1 has its own supervisor folder and its own port. In this mode PHP already runs as you, so the Start, Stop, Terminal, Files and Browser buttons start things directly instead of going through sudo (no entry in /etc/sudoers.d is needed, which is what a machine without administrator rights lacks). Under Apache nothing changes: the same sudo -u you calls as before. In this mode Stop and Restart stop only the agents: the web server that is showing you the page stays up (the Exit dialog’s Terminate and leave is the full shutdown, web server included). One window per edition: close the running one first (Exit) when you switch between the two ways of starting. With the web front on, the server also answers the chat’s progress polls (the “new text of the answer” call, many times a second while an agent writes) itself, without starting PHP, whenever it can see you are signed in and the agent is running; every other case goes to PHP unchanged.

Seeing which runtime is in use

While the optional native parts exist next to the shell ones, the status bar shows what is really running, read from the processes themselves and not from the switch files. Next to each agent’s name a small tag says which loop runs: native (the native loop) or shell (the shell script). The process supervisor is the usual host and is not repeated on every tag; when an agent runs in a tmux session instead, the tag says so (tmux · shell). The native loop’s tag is bold. Hover a tag for the plain-words description, who keeps the loop alive and the process number. A tag is hidden while that agent is not running.

The thin status bar at the very bottom of the window, under the prompt and its buttons, shows the last thing that happened (Ready., Loaded chat: …, the latest system message, a success or an error). It had slipped out of view because the Attach button added a fourth row to the button column; CLEAR, SAVE and Attach now share one row, and the bar is back.

The three labels at the left of the status bar name the agent and its model (Claude · Sonnet 4.6, OpenCode · qwen2.5:7b, Local · Dual); the dot beside each says whether it is running, and the full text is in the hover.

Three one-word tags beside the usage figures, in this order: the native engine (on or off; the file use_engine), the scheduler tick (sup for a supervised job, cron otherwise) and the web server that answered the page you are looking at (apache, the default, or aic for the optional aicserver front on port 8081). Hover each one for its name in plain words. Hover it for the full list: how the loops are hosted, whether the engine program is installed, and which use_native_loop files ask for the native loop. If a tag does not match what you switched on, the loop that is running started before the switch: restart the agents.

The process supervisor (optional, off by default)

By default each agent’s loop (Claude, Gemini, Ollama) runs in its own tmux session. Cockpit can instead run them under aicsupervisor, a small native program (Free Pascal, installed beside the scripts). Nothing changes on screen except the points below.

Switch it on: create an empty file called use_supervisor in your Cockpit data folder (~/scripts/cockpit_data/use_supervisor, or cockpit_data_v1 for V1), then Restart the sessions (or run cockpit_stop.sh and cockpit_start.sh). Switch it off: delete the file and restart. If the supervisor program is missing or does not answer, Cockpit uses tmux exactly as before, and the status block still shows an agent as running if it is running in tmux.

What is different when it is on:

  • A loop that dies comes back. The supervisor restarts it (after a pause that grows from 1 to 30 seconds; after more than ten crashes in two minutes it shows as failed and stays down until you Start again). With tmux a dead loop left a session that still counted as “running” and requests that were never answered.
  • Stop sends the interrupt to the agent’s process group, as Ctrl-C in a terminal does, instead of typing it into a tmux pane. The loop itself carries on (it has an interrupt handler since build 198); an older loop that dies from it is restarted at once.
  • Open session on an agent’s card shows the agent’s live log in a terminal (the lines a tmux pane would have shown) instead of attaching to tmux. You cannot type into it; the loop takes no typing anyway.
  • Edition rule unchanged: V1 and V2 still cannot run together; the other edition’s supervisor is stopped when you switch.
  • The Tools session stays in tmux.
  • The supervisor’s own files (control socket, token, logs: ~/scripts/cockpit_data/supervisor/) are reachable by the web server’s account through the same group arrangement as the tmux socket; nobody else on the machine can read them.

Start it by itself at login (also optional). ~/scripts/cockpit_sup_autostart.sh install (add --edition v1 for V1) writes a systemd user service, starts it, and turns the switch on; no administrator rights are needed. The service regenerates the supervisor’s configuration before each start. cockpit_stop.sh still stops everything for good (a clean stop is not restarted); the next login starts it again. To start at boot without logging in, run once, yourself: sudo loginctl enable-linger $USER. status shows what is installed, print shows the unit without installing anything, remove takes it away (the switch file stays: delete use_supervisor to go back to tmux).

Never two loops for one agent. Two loops reading the same queue would answer every prompt twice. Since build 202 a loop refuses to start when a live loop of the same agent already serves its queue (it says so and exits), cockpit_start.sh ends a leftover tmux loop of an agent it hands to the supervisor, and cockpit_sup_autostart.sh install ends the tmux agent sessions too (the Tools session stays). If you installed the autostart service before build 202 while tmux sessions were running, end them once: tmux -S /var/www/html/cockpit/tmux.sock kill-session -t cockpit_claude (and cockpit_gemini, cockpit_ollama).

The scheduler tick. With the supervisor on, the minute tick of the Jobs panel (scheduler.php, which a crontab line runs today) is also a supervised job: it runs at start and then every 60 seconds, never two at once. If your crontab line is still there, both tick; the scheduler takes a lock, so a job still runs only once.

Receipts — which passage the answer actually used

When retrieved material is put in front of an agent, the answer now cites which passage it drew on. This is what makes Library, Sources and Bookshelf trustworthy at a glance: you can see whether an answer came from your own material or from the model’s memory.

Cockpit also warns when the model is the wrong tool. If a question that the Library can answer is about to go to an embedding model (it makes vectors, it does not answer), a model tuned for code, or one below about 3B parameters (the floor measured for grounded answers), Cockpit says so and offers to switch to a suitable model.

Cockpit also knows when to say nothing. If some items in your library matched loosely but none covers what you actually asked, nothing is added, and the chat says so: “Your library has N loosely related items, but none covers what you asked, so nothing was added.” The agent then answers from its own knowledge instead of leaning on an unrelated passage. An item has to cover at least half of what the question is about, measured against your own library — common words count for little, rare ones for a lot. A library of fewer than twelve items is too small to measure, so this check stands down there.

Dialects — prompts shaped per supplier

Different agents respond best to differently shaped prompts. Retrieved context is now placed where each model actually reads it, wrapped in the structure that supplier prefers. Nothing to configure — it follows the agent catalog.

Audio analysis — measured facts, no model involved

Point Cockpit at a sound file and get measurements: tempo, duration, loudness, peak level and silences. (Musical key is deliberately not reported: the local tools cannot detect it reliably, and a wrong key is worse than none.) These are computed by local audio tooling, not guessed by a language model, so they are reproducible — the same file gives the same numbers every time.

A file that is not audio — a text file, a video with no sound track — is refused with a plain message instead of getting a report that looks like measurements. Lyrics transcription refuses silence, and also a pure tone or noise, which whisper would otherwise answer with a lone full stop.

Sheet music — both directions

  • Sound to notation. Hum, whistle, or play a melody, and Cockpit transcribes it to engraved sheet music as a PDF.
  • Notation to sound. Give it notation and it plays the piece back with a piano-like voice.

Lyrics can be attached to a transcription. Two honest limits, both enforced rather than merely warned about: the transcription is melody only — one line, such as humming or a solo instrument. Cockpit measures whether the recording really is one line, and refuses chords, a band or a full mix with an explanation, instead of engraving a confident wrong tune. And a photograph or scan of sheet music is not supported; reading printed music optically is a different problem, and Cockpit refuses that input with an explanation too. (A melody over a much quieter accompaniment is still transcribed: the melody is what the tool follows.)

Add your own agent, and test it before trusting it

The agent catalog is editable from inside Cockpit. If a new CLI agent appears, you can describe how it is invoked — binary, model flag, how it takes an image, how it likes its prompt — and test it from the editor before putting it on a card. No rebuild, no reinstall, no waiting for a Cockpit release.

Removing an agent you added deletes it; removing your changes to a shipped agent puts it back to its default. If a removed agent was sitting on a card, that card goes back to its default agent (never the same agent on both cards), and Cockpit tells you.

Voice input — choose the microphone, and see it working

Dictation lets you pick which microphone to use and shows a live input level — a bar beside the mic button while you speak — so “nothing happened” is immediately distinguishable from “the wrong device was selected” or “the mic is muted”. See Voice input (offline) for the details.

Language of Cockpit

The translate button beside the font-size picker (top bar, Settings) chooses the language Cockpit is shown in. English is the default. Every label, hint and message in the app can be translated; language packs ship for a few languages but so far cover only a small part, and anything not translated stays English. Buttons keep exactly the size they have in English: a translated label that is too long for its button scrolls slowly inside it instead of stretching it. The choice is remembered per browser. Right-to-left languages (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu and others) are supported: their text is shown and aligned correctly in answers, tools and files; mirroring the whole screen layout is not done yet.

Add a language: open the menu, download the empty template, save it as <code>.json (for example fr.json), fill in _meta and the values, and put it in the lang folder inside your Cockpit data folder (the menu shows the path). Anything left empty stays English. Add ?lang=fr to the address to try it without choosing it. Developers: see lang/README.md.

The voice Language list is separate: it is the language you speak, and offers every language whisper supports (English by default).

Everywhere relay — machines have names

The relay used to identify a rig by its machine id: correct, unreadable, and useless once you have two machines. Each machine now carries a name you choose, and that name is what the relay page lists and what you pick from on your phone.

CLI agents get an isolated configuration

Agents launched by Cockpit now run with their own CLI configuration by default, separate from the one you use in your own terminal. This stops your personal CLI settings leaking into Cockpit’s agents and changing how they answer.

If you want an agent to use your normal setup, Use my global CLI config turns it back on per supplier.

The icon font is local

Cockpit no longer fetches its icon font from Google at page load. The interface draws correctly with no internet connection, and nothing about your use of Cockpit is announced to a third party in order to render a button.

Step-by-step setup for a Linux Mint 22 / Ubuntu 24.04 / Debian 13 / Fedora 44 / Manjaro machine (openSUSE takes the same installer; the package lists are per distro). Each step has a verification checkpoint. Do not skip steps. If a step fails, the Troubleshooting section at the end has fixes.

Before you start

CI-verified — an unattended end-to-end run of install_cockpit.sh passes on a real Linux Mint/Ubuntu runner (GitHub Actions). Hand-tested end to end on fresh Ubuntu 24.04, Fedora 44 Workstation, Debian 13 (XFCE), Manjaro (KDE), openSUSE Tumbleweed (GNOME) and Arch (MATE) VMs, and on Windows 11 (25H2) through WSL2, with every option on (LocalAI, LibreTranslate, Piper, whisper.cpp, Aider, companion tools).

Required

  • Linux Mint 22.x / Ubuntu 24.04 / Debian 13 (or a derivative), Fedora 44 Workstation, or Manjaro/Arch. Arch: the installer does the full pacman -Syu first (keyrings, mirrors), wires php-apache (prefork + php_module + php.ini extensions) and lifts ProtectHome on httpd.service so the web server can reach ~/scripts. On Fedora the installer also sets SELinux so the web server may run your agents (only the httpd_t domain is made permissive; everything else stays enforcing)
  • Sudo access on the machine
  • 4 GB RAM and ~10 GB disk to run Cockpit itself
  • Working internet connection (only needed during setup; cockpit runs offline)

Nothing below is required, and the installer never refuses a machine. Hardware decides only how fast local models run — and local models are one of five supplier classes. Paid CLIs (Claude, Codex, Qwen), free REST workers (Gemini, Groq) and every tool need no GPU at all, so a modest laptop runs Cockpit perfectly well.

Minimum recommendations

Four tiers. None of them is enforced — the installer accepts any machine and tells you what it found.

1. To run Cockpit — 4 GB RAM, ~10 GB disk, no GPU. Everything works except local models: paid CLIs (Claude, Codex, Qwen), free REST workers (Gemini, Groq), tools, projects, chats, the relay. This is a perfectly normal way to use Cockpit.

2. Minimum for local models at usable speed — 8 GB RAM, no GPU needed. Measured: 3B at ~8 tok/s, 1.5B at ~16 tok/s, both above the ~4 tok/s floor where things begin timing out. Core count barely matters — 2 threads measured the same as 12 — because CPU inference is limited by memory bandwidth, not cores. Bookshelf sizes its chapters to 12 KB here so one stays readable in under a minute.

3. Comfortable local models — 4 GB VRAM and 16 GB RAM. Measured: 3B at 58 tok/s, 1.5B at 104. This is the sweet spot for a small card. Do not expect more from it: 7B drops to 5.6 tok/s, and 14B fails rather than crawls. Bookshelf uses 20 KB chapters here (~7s to read one).

4. Larger models — 8 GB VRAM for 7B-class, 12 GB+ for 14B-class. Inferred from how much VRAM a model needs to avoid spilling onto the CPU; not measured here, since the test machine has 4 GB.

The honest summary: Cockpit needs very little. Local models are what want hardware, and even they are usable with no GPU at all as long as you stay at 3B or below.

How fast will local models be here?

Measured on a 4 GB GPU (AMD RX 6400) and a 12-core CPU, generation tokens per second:

Model 4 GB GPU CPU only (no GPU)
1.5B 104 16
3B 58 8
3.8B 12 6
7B 5.6 3.7
14B 2.3 1.8

Read it as: above ~10 tok/s feels live (faster than you read); below ~4 tok/s things start timing out rather than merely feeling slow.

What you have What to expect
No GPU, modern multi-core Everything works. Local models up to 3B are
CPU comfortable. 7B and larger will be painfully slow.
4 GB VRAM 3B-class models are the sweet spot (58 tok/s).
7B runs but drags; 14B will time out on long
answers — it is not slow, it fails.
8 GB VRAM 7B-class comfortably.
12 GB+ VRAM 14B-class comfortably.
RAM 16 GB is comfortable; 32 GB if you want several
models resident or Dual mode.

Two measured details worth knowing. The cliff is between 3B and 3.8B on a 4 GB card — 58 to 12 tok/s — because the model stops fitting in VRAM and spills onto the CPU. And a 4 GB card only earns its keep up to 3B: at 7B it is just 1.5x faster than the CPU, at 14B 1.3x, because by then most layers are running on the CPU anyway.

If your machine is below these, install anyway. Cockpit will tell you what it detected, default the model downloads to none so you are not pulling multi-GB files that will crawl, and let you pick. Everything except local model speed is unaffected.

Features that read long text size themselves to your hardware: Bookshelf splits a book into chapters small enough for the machine that will read them (12 KB with no GPU, 20 KB on a 4 GB card, 40 KB above that), so a chapter stays readable instead of taking minutes.

Optional but useful

  • A GPU, for local models only. Nothing else uses it. A 4 GB card makes 3B-class models comfortable (58 tok/s measured); 8 GB suits 7B, 12 GB+ suits 14B. Dual mode needs enough for both models resident at once. The app detects your real GPU/VRAM at install time (AMD and NVIDIA) and sizes the local-model offers to it. With no GPU, local models still run on the CPU up to about 3B — see How fast will local models be here?
  • A non-default home directory layout — the cockpit derives your home directory from the environment, so a standard /home/<you> works with no edits. If your projects live somewhere unusual (a second disk, a network mount), point projects_root at it in paths.json or from the Library/Config tab

What the installer sends, and how to stop it

install_cockpit.sh sends one anonymous line when it starts — OS, distro, architecture, package manager, coarse hardware, and the installer’s own version — and uses the reply to tell you whether a newer release exists. No username, no file paths, no file contents, no IP. It happens before the edition prompt because one installer serves every edition, so at that moment there is no choice yet to respect.

Choosing Stand-alone (V1) ends it there: that line plus the record of your choice are the last things sent, and at the end you are asked once, knowing the install worked, whether to send a single anonymous “it succeeded” line. Decline and nothing is sent and nothing asks again. V2/Both additionally report install progress and errors, so broken installs can be found and fixed.

To send nothing at all, set the environment variable before running it:

COCKPIT_NO_TELEMETRY=1 sudo -E bash install_cockpit.sh

(The manual steps in this guide send nothing regardless — there is no installer involved.)

What you should download before running these steps

Get this bundle ready in ~/Downloads/:

The installer — the setup window

The cockpit ships an automated install_cockpit.sh that does everything below end-to-end. This is the normal path; the numbered steps after it are the manual sequence, for understanding what happens or for finishing by hand if it stops.

  • A setup window, then it runs. On a desktop the script opens a wizard (ckdialog, shipped in the bundle, Free Pascal + GTK 3): edition, install user, projects folder, optional CLIs, models sized to the hardware it detects, media tools, desktop shortcut, logins — every choice first, a summary page, one Install button. The system password is asked once, in a dialog (sudo). A progress window then follows the install log phase by phase and says Done. It opens light or dark to match the desktop; the ☾/☀ button switches, and the choice is remembered. Over SSH, or with COCKPIT_TUI=1, the same questions are asked in the terminal up front; a question left alone for 10 minutes takes the default shown.
  • Full edition: the account comes first. The first local login on a machine takes your Cockpit account name — sign in with an existing account or register a free one (human check) inside the setup; the app’s own login is created with that name. Stand-alone asks only for a local login.
  • Interrupted? Re-run it. It remembers every answer (never passwords) in ~/.local/state/ai-cockpit/install.state and asks Continue or Start anew. Components it finds already on the machine — Node, Ollama, LocalAI, LibreTranslate, Piper, whisper.cpp, Aider, Goose/opencode, models, the companion tools — are listed on a Keep page: ticked ones are left as they are, unticked ones are redone. Re-running over a finished install is the upgrade path: same answers remembered, same Keep page, files refreshed from the bundle.
  • Everything is logged to ~/cockpit-install.log — send that file when reporting a problem. The final screen lists it with the web-server log.
  • Fedora: the installer also sets SELinux so the web server may run your agents — only the httpd_t domain is made permissive (denials are logged, not enforced); every other domain stays enforcing. Binaries under ~/.local/bin get the bin_t label.
  • Tested as a stranger would, on fresh Ubuntu 24.04, Fedora 44 Workstation, Debian 13, Manjaro, openSUSE Tumbleweed and Arch (MATE) VMs with every option on. Arch: the http account ships expired and httpd.service sets NoNewPrivileges — the installer lifts both, or nothing the app launches via sudo can start. openSUSE: Tumbleweed enforces SELinux and its web server runs as wwwrun:www — the installer handles both.

This guide walks through the manual sequence — useful if you want to understand what’s happening or if the auto-installer fails partway.

Installing on macOS / Windows

Steps 1–12 below are written for Linux Mint/Ubuntu. Cockpit itself is just Apache + PHP + Bash + tmux — it runs the same way on any OS that can provide those, with the caveats below.

macOS

TESTED macOS installs end to end on Apple Silicon, verified 25 September 2026: the real installer runs unattended to Installation complete, httpd serves the app (HTTP 200), the VERSION file lands, and the runtime scripts pass a BSD-userland check.

This guide previously claimed macOS was CI-tested when it was not — the weekly job was reporting a pass while the installer aborted part-way through, because it exited with a success status after dying. Making the job assert completion rather than trust the exit code exposed five real faults, all now fixed:

  • stat -c is GNU-only, and under set -e a failed command substitution aborts the script — the install ended silently after the Edition phase.
  • The Homebrew httpd.conf was looked for at two paths that do not exist on a Mac, so the port move, the Cockpit alias and the PHP module were all skipped. httpd then came up healthy serving nothing.
  • ${var,,} and ${var^^} are bash 4; macOS still ships bash 3.2 as /bin/bash. This killed the install at Phase 5b — and ${1,,} in one helper survived a build guard added to catch exactly that, because the guard’s pattern could not match a positional parameter.
  • Three sed -i calls bypassed the script’s own portable helper. On BSD that takes the next argument as a backup suffix, so the agent loop would have misbehaved on every Mac, quietly.

What the run does and does not prove: it installs, starts httpd and checks the app answers. It does not drive the interface.

There is no separate macOS installer — the old install_cockpit_macos.sh was retired because it had genuine bugs on Apple Silicon and drifted from the Linux script.

Genuinely native-capable — no virtualization needed. Apple removed PHP and disabled Apache by default since macOS 12, but both install cleanly via Homebrew:

# 1. Install Homebrew if you don't have it: https://brew.sh
brew install httpd php tmux ffmpeg pandoc

# 2. whisper.cpp — build with the Metal backend (not Vulkan, that's Linux-only)
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp
cd whisper.cpp && make

# 3. Ollama — official native app, Apple Silicon Metal-accelerated
#    https://ollama.com/download/mac

# 4. Start Apache (httpd), point its docroot at the cockpit-bundle folder,
#    same as Step 5–6 below — paths differ slightly (/opt/homebrew/... on
#    Apple Silicon, /usr/local/... on Intel) but the steps are the same.

Everything else — Steps 6 through 12 — is identical to the Linux instructions once Apache/PHP/tmux are running. Apple Silicon (M-series) is the architecture being worked on; Intel Macs are not tested at all.

Windows — via WSL2 (not native)

TESTED Hand-tested end to end on a fresh Windows 11 25H2 machine: install_windows.ps1, then the normal Linux installer inside WSL, then the Cockpit window opened from the Windows Start menu. Findings from that run are folded into the script and the notes below.

Native Windows can't run this stack as-is — agent_loop.sh is built around tmux, which has no real Windows equivalent. The supported path is WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux): a real Ubuntu environment running alongside Windows. Cockpit then runs in its own window (the same native WebKitGTK window as on Linux, shown by WSLg), opened from a Windows Start-menu / Desktop shortcut; its Terminal, Files and Browser buttons open gnome-terminal, Nautilus and the Cockpit Browser as ordinary windows next to your Windows apps.

Recommended — one-click installer

Download the bundle with Edge from the download page, right-click cockpit_install.tar.gz → Extract All (Windows 11 unpacks .tar.gz natively), then run install_windows.ps1 from the extracted cockpit folder in an elevated PowerShell:

# Start → type powershell → "Run as administrator", then:
cd $HOME\Downloads\cockpit_install\cockpit
powershell -ep bypass .\install_windows.ps1

It does the whole Windows side: enables WSL2 and installs Ubuntu-24.04 (offers the one reboot Windows needs, and continues where it left off when you run it again), creates the Linux user cockpit unattended (shows its random password once — that is the password sudo asks for inside WSL, not your Windows one), keeps systemd on inside the distro, writes %USERPROFILE%\.wslconfig (vmIdleTimeout=-1 so Cockpit stays up when no terminal is open, networkingMode=mirrored so localhost reaches it from every Windows browser), installs VS Code + its WSL extension, and puts an AI Cockpit shortcut in the Start menu and on the Desktop.

It does not run install_cockpit.sh for you. When it finishes it prints the exact next line — open the Ubuntu-24.04 app and paste it:

cp -r /mnt/c/Users/<you>/Downloads/cockpit_install/cockpit ~/cockpit && cd ~/cockpit && bash install_cockpit.sh

From there it is the Linux installer, setup window included (WSLg shows it). Then click AI Cockpit on the Desktop.

Manual path (if you'd rather not run the script)

# 1. Install WSL2 + Ubuntu (PowerShell, as Administrator)
wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04

# 2. Reboot when prompted, then open the new "Ubuntu-24.04" Start Menu entry
#    and finish the Ubuntu first-run (create a Linux username/password —
#    unrelated to your Windows login).

# 3. In PowerShell, write %USERPROFILE%\.wslconfig with these two lines,
#    then run  wsl --shutdown  once:
#      [wsl2]
#      vmIdleTimeout=-1
#      networkingMode=mirrored
#    (without them WSL stops Cockpit a minute after the last terminal closes,
#    and Edge/Chrome cannot reach http://localhost/cockpit/ — it is
#    forwarded on IPv6 only in the default NAT mode.)

# 4. Inside the Ubuntu shell, follow Steps 1–12 of this guide exactly
#    as written — it's a real Ubuntu 24.04, nothing Windows-specific
#    from here on. Open Cockpit with  cockpit-start  (its own window), or
#    from your Windows browser at http://localhost/cockpit/  (type the
#    http:// — Edge silently upgrades bare addresses to https).

Then install VS Code + its "WSL" (Remote-WSL) extension yourself, and use Ctrl+Shift+P → "WSL: Connect to WSL" to open project folders with full native-tool convenience at full WSL-native filesystem speed — this is the setup we recommend project files live under (inside WSL's own filesystem), not on the Windows side reached via /mnt/c/..., which has real I/O overhead for the kind of many-small-file CRUD Cockpit's agents do.

Ollama — run it natively on Windows, not inside WSL. Ollama has a real native Windows installer with full NVIDIA CUDA GPU support — better performance than running it inside the WSL2 virtual machine. Install it normally from ollama.com/download/windows, then point Cockpit's Ollama connection (inside WSL) at the Windows host's IP instead of localhost:

# Inside WSL, find the Windows host IP:
cat /etc/resolv.conf | grep nameserver
# → use that IP with Ollama's port, e.g. http://172.x.x.x:11434
# Set OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 on the Windows side (System Environment
# Variables) so it accepts connections from WSL, not just localhost.

Optional — stable machine identity across WSL reinstalls

WSL2's own machine identity is not stable — reinstalling the Ubuntu distro (or certain Windows updates) resets it, which would make Cockpit's SaaS licensing think it's a brand-new machine each time. To avoid that, copy the Windows-native cockpit_auth.exe build to a fixed path Windows and WSL can both see, and Cockpit will automatically prefer it for machine identification (falls back to the normal Linux binary if this isn't set up — nothing breaks either way):

# From Windows (PowerShell or File Explorer):
mkdir C:\CockpitAuth
copy cockpit_auth.exe C:\CockpitAuth\cockpit_auth.exe
# That's it — Cockpit (running in WSL) detects WSL automatically and
# reaches this .exe at /mnt/c/CockpitAuth/cockpit_auth.exe.

Alternative for Windows or macOS — Docker

NOT TESTED YET Written and reviewed carefully, but this bundle hasn't actually been built/run end-to-end yet — please let us know how it goes if you try it.

One Dockerfile + docker-compose.yml, same on both OSes — Docker Desktop already runs on WSL2 (Windows) or Apple's virtualization framework (macOS), so this sidesteps writing separate native/WSL2/Homebrew instructions per OS. Ollama and LocalAI both run inside the same container as Cockpit, not as separate ones — the app's PHP backends call both at hardcoded local addresses (127.0.0.1:11434 / 127.0.0.1:8080), not a configurable host, so split containers wouldn't be reachable. Both agents' models persist in their own named Docker volumes across rebuilds.

Download the Docker bundle from the download page (separate small zip — Dockerfile, compose file, entrypoint script, and a step-by-step README; it doesn't duplicate the app itself, you extract the main tarball's web/ folder alongside it). Not yet published to Docker Hub, so you build locally:

docker compose build      # first time, or after updating web/
docker compose up -d
# One-time: authenticate the agent CLIs
docker compose exec cockpit su - cockpit -c claude
docker compose exec cockpit su - cockpit -c gemini
# Then open in your normal browser:
# http://localhost:8080

GPU passthrough to Ollama only works via Docker on a Linux host with the NVIDIA Container Toolkit (uncomment the deploy: block in docker-compose.yml) — Docker Desktop on Windows/macOS doesn't pass a GPU through to containers, so Ollama runs CPU-only there, fine for small (1–4B) models.

Raspberry Pi / ARM Linux

CI-verified — an unattended end-to-end run of install_cockpit.sh passes on a real ARM64 runner (GitHub Actions).

A Pi running 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS (Debian-based) is full, real Linux — Apache, PHP, bash, and tmux all work exactly as they do on any x86_64 Linux box. Steps 1–12 of this guide apply unchanged — there's no separate "Pi edition" of the install process. A Pi is also a legitimate, popular way to host Ollama itself as a small always-on local model server, even for other machines on your network to reach.

The one Pi-specific piece is cockpit_auth — the compiled SaaS-licensing binary needs its own ARM build (a Pi can't run the x86_64 binary). That build now exists — see the download page for the ARM Linux binary alongside the x86_64/Windows/macOS ones.

Realistic expectations: a Pi 4/5 with 8GB RAM can run small Ollama models (1–4B parameters) at reasonable speed for CRUD-style combo work; it is not going to run anything comparable to a desktop GPU for larger models — treat it as a small-model or remote-Ollama-target machine, not a general-purpose Cockpit workstation replacement.

Everywhere — remote access from your phone

The Everywhere tier lets a phone or any other browser talk to a Cockpit already running on your home rig, without port-forwarding or a static IP. Your rig has no open port; both sides poll a small queue on cockpit.ruggi.site over plain HTTPS — nothing to configure on your router.

Status: built, not yet deployed. The relay server, the home-rig poller, and the phone page all exist in the codebase as of this guide's last update, but the database schema hasn't been run against the live server yet and none of it has been tested end-to-end. Treat this section as "how it will work", not a guarantee it's live right now.

One-time setup on your home rig

  1. Make sure your account is signed in and has the Max plan (or the Everywhere add-on) — check Settings → Account.

  2. Create ~/scripts/cockpit_data/relay_poller_credentials.json with your local Cockpit login (the same username/password you use to open the web UI on this machine):

    {"username": "your-local-username", "password": "your-local-password"}

                            # Should show "PHP Version => 8.3.x"

                            # Should show current time in your zone

Keep the working folders private

Apache listens on every network interface and, left alone, lists the contents of any folder and serves any file in it. For Cockpit that would expose responses/ and queue/ (the agents’ replies and the queued prompts) to everyone on your network without a login. The automated installer closes this for you; if you set Apache up by hand, install the same rule:

sudo bash Installs/apache/install_security_conf.sh
# Both of these should now say 403:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost/cockpit/responses/
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost/cockpit/paths.json

It tests the configuration before reloading and puts everything back if the test fails. The rule never touches anything that is not under a cockpit or cockpit-v1 folder.

Raising the upload size limit

PHP ships with upload_max_filesize = 2M and post_max_size = 8M. Above that, PHP does not complain: the upload just arrives empty, and the feature answers “No audio uploaded” or “No file uploaded”. On a stock install that meant a voice note longer than about a minute, a video for the transcriber, or a larger chat import was silently dropped. The automated installer raises both limits to 1 GB for Cockpit’s folders only. By hand:

# Apache with mod_php (Debian, Ubuntu, Mint):
sudo bash Installs/apache/install_php_conf.sh

# PHP-FPM or php-cgi: nothing to install --- Cockpit ships a .user.ini beside
# index.html with the same two values (upload_max_filesize, post_max_size).
# Check what PHP actually uses for Cockpit's folder:
curl -s http://localhost/cockpit/auth.php?action=check >/dev/null   # (any PHP page)
php -i | grep -E 'upload_max_filesize|post_max_size'                 # the CLI's own values, for comparison

Files that travel inside the page’s own data (chat attachments up to 50 MB, books up to 80 MB, personal-archive scans up to 25 MB) are limited by PHP’s memory, not by these two settings; Cockpit raises that limit itself for those requests.

Step 7 — Permissions and sudoers

Apache (running as www-data) needs read access to the cockpit data and tmux socket. Your user (running as dario) needs write access. The bridge between these is the www-data group.

# Add www-data group membership for shared file access

sudo chmod -R g+rX /var/www/html/cockpit/

sudo chmod -R g+rwX ~/scripts/cockpit_data/

# tmux socket lives in /tmp; needs group access from www-data
# (cockpit_start.sh creates this on each run with the right perms)

# Add www-data to your group so it can read your home dir prefix
sudo usermod -a -G $USER www-data

# Allow www-data to invoke the cockpit_*.sh scripts without password
sudo bash -c 'cat > /etc/sudoers.d/cockpit' << EOF
www-data ALL=(${USER}) NOPASSWD: ${HOME}/scripts/cockpit_start.sh
www-data ALL=(${USER}) NOPASSWD: ${HOME}/scripts/cockpit_stop.sh

sudo chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/cockpit

Step 10b — Companion tools (installed for you)

The scripted installer also sets up two small command-line suites that are not part of Cockpit itself but ship with it. They are ordinary tools on your PATH, with their own --help and man pages, and Cockpit never depends on them — remove them and nothing in the app changes.

  • ftpsuite (ftpush, ftpull, ftps-cli, ftps-gui) — scripted file transfer to a site you own. Sites and local-to-remote path pairs live in a JSON config, so one tool serves several sites: ftpush --add-site, then ftpush --add-pair, then ftpush -p1 <files>. Credentials stay in that config (chmod 600) and are never passed on the command line.
  • secrets (secrets, secrets-cli, secrets-gui) — an encrypted store for your own keys and logins, held as a GPG-encrypted Markdown file. Several stores, several templates, a template editor, and a re-key command for rotating the passphrase without leaving old copies behind. secrets init creates the first store.

Both have dark/light themes in their GUIs and man ftpush / man secrets for the details. If you are following the manual steps in this guide, neither is installed — fetch them from the tools pages on the site if you want them.

Troubleshooting

Apache returns 403 Forbidden

# Permissions on the cockpit directory
sudo chown -R dario:www-data /var/www/html/cockpit/
sudo chmod -R g+rX /var/www/html/cockpit/

# Apache config — make sure /var/www/html is allowed
grep -A3 "Directory /var/www/" /etc/apache2/apache2.conf
                            # Should include "Require all granted"

“Bridge.php returned no response”

The PHP error log usually has the answer:

sudo tail -50 /var/log/apache2/error.log

Common causes:

  • php-curl missing: sudo nala install php8.3-curl && sudo systemctl restart apache2
  • paths.json missing or corrupt: re-copy from the bundle
  • bridge.php has a syntax error: php -l /var/www/html/cockpit/bridge.php

“Agent session not found in tmux”

# Check what sessions exist
tmux -S /tmp/cockpit_tmux.sock ls 2>&1

# If empty, restart cockpit
~/scripts/cockpit_stop.sh && ~/scripts/cockpit_start.sh

# If permission denied, the socket has wrong group
sudo chgrp www-data /tmp/cockpit_tmux.sock
sudo chmod 660 /tmp/cockpit_tmux.sock

Cockpit opens in a browser instead of its own window

cockpit_shell could not run here. Ask it why:

~/scripts/cockpit_shell --check
  • cannot load libwebkit2gtk-4.1.so.0 — install the runtime: sudo apt install libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0 (Arch: webkit2gtk-4.1, Fedora: webkit2gtk4.1, openSUSE: libwebkit2gtk-4_1-0).
  • cannot execute binary file — the prebuilt binary is x86-64; rebuild it for this CPU with bash ~/scripts/cockpit_shell_src/build.sh ~/scripts/cockpit_shell (needs fpc).
  • Everything else: tail -20 ~/.cache/cockpit_shell.log.

The window says Cockpit did not start

The window brings the stack up itself and reports when that fails. Run the same thing in a terminal to see the error:

cockpit-start

Usual causes: Apache not installed or its port taken, the sudoers rule from Step 7 missing, or a full disk. COCKPIT_NO_VERIFY=1 cockpit-start skips the manifest check if that is what refuses to load the app (then use ~/scripts/cockpit_restore.sh to put the shipped files back).

Ctrl+Alt+C does nothing

  • Under Wayland the compositor owns shortcuts: add one for cockpit-start --toggle in the desktop’s keyboard settings.
  • Another application may already hold the combination — pick a different one: ~/scripts/install_hotkey.sh "<Super>c".
  • Check what is registered: gsettings get org.cinnamon.desktop.keybindings custom-list (Cinnamon) or the desktop’s Keyboard settings.

No tray icon

GNOME Shell shows tray icons only with the AppIndicator extension (sudo apt install gnome-shell-extension-appindicator, then enable it and log out and in). KDE, XFCE, Cinnamon and MATE show it as is. Notifications work regardless. ### Claude / Gemini OAuth fails

Both CLIs need a working browser OAuth flow:

# From a desktop environment with a browser available
claude   # Will print an auth URL; open it in your browser, sign in
gemini   # Same flow, separate auth

If you’re SSHing in headlessly, you’ll need to do the auth on the machine’s actual desktop session first.

You sign in once, in your own ~/.claude. Agents the cockpit starts run against a cockpit-owned config directory with your credential file symlinked in, so they use that same login and a refreshed token is written back to the real file.

The cockpit’s agents answer in someone else’s voice

Symptom: answers come back in a style the cockpit never asked for — clipped, themed, or following house rules you set somewhere else — while the Style selector says something different.

Cause: a SessionStart hook or plugin in your personal CLI config (~/.claude/settings.json). It is injected before the cockpit’s own prompt, so nothing inside the cockpit can override it.

Fix: nothing to do — since build 97 the cockpit’s agents run against an isolated config and never see it. If you are on an older build, or you switched the Use my global CLI config capability on, turn that capability off (Settings –> Capabilities) or disable the hook in your own config.

Ollama: “no models” in cockpit dropdown

# Confirm models exist
ollama list

# If empty, pull the defaults:
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:1.5b

# Confirm OLLAMA_MODELS is being honored
ls ~/ollama/models/  # Should show downloaded blobs

# If models live in /usr/share/ollama/.ollama/, the systemd override didn't apply
sudo systemctl edit ollama.service   # Re-set the Environment line
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart ollama

LocalAI: “no models” in cockpit dropdown

# Confirm the service is actually running
systemctl status localai

# Confirm models exist
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/models

# If empty, pull a default
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/models/apply \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"id":"qwen3-1.7b"}'

# Confirm LOCALAI_MODELS_PATH is being honored
ls ~/localai/models/  # Should show downloaded files

# If the service won't start, check the unit for typos in the paths
systemctl cat localai.service
journalctl -u localai -n 50 --no-pager

Tool detection always says “not found”

# Verify the binaries are in PATH that Apache can see
sudo -u www-data which ffmpeg
sudo -u www-data which whisper
sudo -u www-data which pandoc

# If www-data can't see them but you can, the binaries are in a path
# www-data doesn't search. Either:
#   (a) Use Tools settings to set absolute path
#   (b) Add the path to /etc/environment so it's system-wide

Workers HTTP 401 / 403

API key issue. Re-generate the key on the provider’s site, paste it into Workers settings, save.

Workers HTTP 429

Rate limited. Wait a few minutes or switch providers. The cockpit’s usage tracker shows your call counts per provider in the settings modal.

Plans tab is empty after Plan-mode submit

Check the chat for system messages like “Plan creation failed”. Most common cause is one of the voter agents being unauthenticated or unreachable. Run claude --print "test" and gemini --prompt "test" from a terminal to confirm both are working.

IPv6 / wget bug on Linux Mint

A known bug — wget defaults to IPv6 and times out on some Mint installs. Already absorbed into cockpit_start.sh, but if you see the symptom elsewhere:

# Force IPv4 globally for wget
echo 'inet4_only = on' >> ~/.wgetrc

Apache logs filling up

The cockpit polls the bridge every 200 ms during streams, which generates a lot of access-log entries. If you don’t need them:

# Disable access logging for /cockpit/bridge.php specifically
sudo bash -c 'cat > /etc/apache2/conf-available/cockpit-quiet.conf' << 'EOF'
SetEnvIf Request_URI "/cockpit/bridge\.php" cockpit_quiet
CustomLog ${APACHE_LOG_DIR}/access.log combined env=!cockpit_quiet
EOF
sudo a2enconf cockpit-quiet
sudo systemctl reload apache2

Uninstall

If you ever need to wipe the cockpit:

# Stop everything
~/scripts/cockpit_stop.sh 2>/dev/null

# Web root
sudo rm -rf /var/www/html/cockpit/

# Scripts
rm -rf ~/scripts/cockpit_*.sh ~/scripts/agent_loop.sh ~/scripts/crud_executor.sh ~/scripts/install_capabilities.sh

# Data (this is destructive — projects under here are gone forever)
# Keep this if you want to preserve your chats/library/snippets
rm -rf ~/scripts/cockpit_data/

# Sudoers fragment
sudo rm /etc/sudoers.d/cockpit

# Apache PHP override (optional — only do this if no other PHP apps need it)
sudo rm /etc/php/8.3/apache2/conf.d/99-cockpit.ini
sudo systemctl restart apache2

The Claude / Gemini / Ollama / LocalAI installations stay — they’re independent of the cockpit and you may want them for direct use. LocalAI's systemd service (localai.service) also stays enabled; disable it yourself with sudo systemctl disable --now localai if you no longer want it running.

That’s it. If you’ve followed all 12 steps, you have a fully working AI Cockpit. The User Guide covers what to do once it’s running.

Update — June 2026: Additional setup for new features

The base install above is unchanged. These extra steps enable features added later. All are optional — the cockpit runs without them, and each feature degrades gracefully (with a hint) when its tool is missing.

A. uv / uvx — for MCP capabilities (Claude & Gemini)

Capabilities that run an MCP server (e.g. the bundled time capability) launch it via uvx, which ships with uv (Astral’s Python tool).

# Official installer (adds ~/.local/bin to PATH)
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
# new shell, then verify:
uvx --version
  • One-time network needed; after that uvx <server> is cached.
  • Must be on the PATH the agents see — after installing, restart the cockpit (Stop → Start) so the agent sessions pick up the new PATH.
  • npx (from Node, Step 2) covers npm-based MCP servers and needs no extra setup.

B. whisper.cpp + a model — for offline voice input

The mic Voice button transcodes mic audio with ffmpeg (already installed) and transcribes it locally with whisper.cpp.

# The installer's optional whisper.cpp step does all of this for you, into
# ~/ai-tools/whisper.cpp (the one place Cockpit looks first). By hand:
mkdir -p ~/ai-tools && git clone https://github.com/ggerganov/whisper.cpp ~/ai-tools/whisper.cpp
cd ~/ai-tools/whisper.cpp
cmake -B build && cmake --build build -j --config Release
# Grab a model — base is fast; large-v3-turbo is the best balance and fits a 4 GB GPU:
./models/download-ggml-model.sh large-v3-turbo
  • The cockpit auto-detects the binary (whisper-cli). It uses the model pinned in cockpit_data/whisper_config.json — the installer writes the one you chose — and with none pinned it falls back to the largest installed ggml-*.bin. You can also pick a model per dictation in the voice options. To pin specific paths, set bin, model, language in that file.
  • Build with GPU support to use an AMD/NVIDIA card; CPU is fine for short clips.
  • The web tier (www-data) must be able to read the binary + model under your home dir. If transcription says “permission denied”: chmod -R a+rX ~/ai-tools/whisper.cpp.

C. Prism (syntax highlighting) — already vendored

No install needed. prism.js ships in the web root (offline, MIT). It is loaded with Prism.manual = true so it only highlights the cockpit’s code editor, not the chat console.

D. New config files (created on first use)

Under cockpit_data/: directives_global*.md, directives_config.json, claude_controls.json, gemini_controls.json, whisper_config.json, global_caps.json, help.json. All are plain JSON/Markdown and editable in-app (the relevant panel’s edit button opens them in the floating editor).

Update — September 2026: Setup for the new features

The installer handles all of this on a supported Linux distribution — this section is for people installing by hand, or checking why one feature is greyed out when the rest work.

E. Bookshelf — reading books

sudo apt install pandoc          # epub, docx, odt, fb2
sudo apt install calibre         # optional: mobi/azw and friends

pandoc covers the common formats and is already installed for the guides. calibre is only needed for Amazon-style formats; it is a large package, and Bookshelf works without it for everything pandoc reads. Without either, the Bookshelf panel will say so rather than silently accepting a file it cannot split.

F. PDF Vision — rendering pages as images

sudo apt install poppler-utils   # provides pdftoppm

Text extraction needs nothing extra; rendering the pages (for diagrams, scans and drawn tables) uses pdftoppm. Pair it with an agent that can actually accept an image — see Vision dispatch in the User Guide.

G. Audio analysis and sheet music

sudo apt install ffmpeg sox aubio-tools lilypond timidity
  • ffmpeg, sox — decoding and level/loudness measurement.
  • aubio-tools — aubiotrack, aubionotes, aubioonset: tempo, pitch and onset detection. These are measurements, not model guesses.
  • lilypond — engraves detected notes into a sheet-music PDF.
  • timidity — plays notation back with a piano-like voice.

Each tool preset checks for its own binary and reports the missing one by name, so a partial install degrades to a clear message rather than an obscure failure.

H. Intercom — the hands-free loop

Intercom needs both halves of the voice path, and both are already covered above: whisper.cpp (section B) to hear you, and piper to answer. The installer offers piper as its own phase; by hand it lives in ~/ai-tools/piper (Installs/install_piper.sh).

For a language piper has no voice for, espeak-ng is used as the fallback and is installed alongside it.

If dictation works but Intercom does not speak back, piper is the missing piece — not whisper.

I. Isolated CLI configuration

Agents launched by Cockpit now get their own CLI config directory by default, so your personal terminal settings do not change how Cockpit’s agents answer. Credentials are shared by reference, so you do not have to sign in twice.

To put a supplier back on your own configuration, enable Use my global CLI config for that supplier in its slot settings.

J. Everywhere relay — naming a machine

Each rig now reports a name with its heartbeat, and the relay lists rigs by that name instead of a 32-character machine id. Set it from the account panel; it is sent on every heartbeat, so nothing has to be re-paired when it changes.
