autopilot-cruise.title: Autopilot Cruise
autopilot-cruise.body:
Autopilot Cruise lets Cockpit fly a whole task. Type a goal in the prompt box and press flight PLAN in the Hive section of the left sidebar: a planner breaks it into steps, picks the best agent/model for each, and runs them as a durable, resumable chain (checkpointed, auto-recovering if the app crashes or the tab closes). The answer lands back in your chat.

A fast-path skips planning for trivial one-line messages. Enter always does classic dispatch to the agent you picked — there is no mode to remember and nothing hidden that changes what your keyboard does. If you would rather read the steps before anything runs, open Chains and use link Draft a plan from the prompt box, which leaves the chain as a Proposal until you press Run. (Basic-tier feature; open free during beta.)

autocognition.title: AutoCognition (agent bus)
autocognition.body: AutoCognition is the brain under Cruise — a local multi-agent bus your agents share, opened from the hive panel. Agents advertise presence and can see, message, and call each other; you get durable task chains with a board, checkpoints, granularity, and auto-resume-on-kill; capability routing (a step marked auto goes to the best-fit agent); quorum voting (several models answer, a judge picks); a consent-gated broker + approvals queue; and one-click turn any Power Combo into a durable chain. Everything runs locally. (Pro-tier feature; open free during beta.)

clock.title: Clock card
clock.body: The clock card shows the local time, date, ISO week, time zone and, below, the account server's time. Hover for the detail card (day of year, UTC offset, week, server offset). The date and zone come from your desktop; the server line tells you how far apart the two clocks are, which matters for quota resets and licence dates.

artifacts.title: Artifacts
artifacts.body:
Everything this project produced, in one list: files an agent wrote (CRUD blocks or its own tools), images/audio/video you generated, tool outputs (pandoc, ffmpeg…), transcripts, and code approved into Snippets or Sources.

  • Each row shows size, when, where it came from, and — when the chat log named the file — which chat, agent and model: made by when a tool reported writing the file with its full path, mentioned by when a chat only talked about it (a label read from the conversation, not a record).
  • Open hands the file to the desktop app, folder reveals it, delete removes it from disk.
  • Filter by kind (documents, code, images, audio, video, data).

The tab only aggregates: artifacts are ordinary files in your project folder and your Cockpit data folder, editable and usable outside Cockpit.

inherit_cli_config.title: Use my global CLI config
inherit_cli_config.body:
Off by default. With it off, a CLI agent Cockpit starts (Claude Code) runs against an isolated, Cockpit-owned config directory holding only your login — your personal hooks, plugins, skills and global memory are not loaded, so the answers are shaped by Cockpit's Mode and Style alone.

Turn it on to deliberately share your own setup with the agents.

Why it exists: a caveman-mode SessionStart hook installed for the terminal was silently rewriting every Cockpit answer on the developer's own machine while the Style selector said "Build (default)". Your login is symlinked into the isolated directory, so you never sign in twice and refreshed tokens still reach the real credential file.

margin.title: Margin — ask for a change to just these lines
margin.body:
Select lines in the file viewer and a Margin button appears. Say what should change; the agent gets those exact lines plus your note and answers with a replacement.

Nothing is written until you press Apply. You see the current lines beside the proposed ones, and the write goes through the same path the editor uses.

Why it is built this way: the anchor (file + line range + the exact text) travels with the request, so the agent never has to find the place again and cannot drift onto a similar passage. Only the replacement is asked for — a model re-emitting a whole file to change three lines loses things nobody reviewed. And before writing, the file is read again and the anchor re-checked: if those lines have changed, moved, or now appear twice, the write is refused rather than guessed.

After Apply the open preview re-reads the file so you see the change at once. The viewer header also has a refresh button that re-reads the file from disk whenever something else changed it.

dossier.title: Dossier — a researched answer with sources you can check
dossier.body:
Ask a question. Cockpit searches several framings of it, reads the pages it finds, and hands the active agent a numbered source pack with one instruction: answer from these and cite them. The report is saved into the project as Markdown, so it appears in Artifacts.

Why Cockpit does the searching: asking an agent to run its own search loop depends on it following instructions for several turns — a small local model will not, and a large one costs a round trip per page. Gathering here means the same question fetches the same pages whichever agent writes the report.

What it is not: a literature review. It reads the first pages a search engine returns. The sources are listed precisely so you can judge them, and the report is told to say where sources disagree or fall silent rather than filling the gap from memory.

Needs the Web Search capability; one page per site, so ten results from one domain cannot crowd out the rest.

Status: the first step is a web search, and public search engines increasingly refuse automated queries — on some networks Dossier comes back empty. It is paused until it can draw on sources that do not depend on them.

profile.title: Profile — what every agent should know about you
profile.body:
Durable facts about you: units, language, timezone, how you like answers, what you are building. Sent with every prompt, so every agent starts knowing them.

Not the same as Rules/Directives. Those say how an agent should behave; this says who it is working with. Separate files and separate editors, because you edit them on different occasions.

Two ways in: the editor (topbar → Profile), or the badge button on any message — select the part worth keeping and it is appended as one line.

Capped at 4 KB on purpose. It rides on every request: a profile that grows into an essay taxes every prompt and crowds out the actual question. Duplicate lines are refused, and when it is full Cockpit says so instead of quietly dropping what you added.

Stored as plain Markdown in cockpit_data/profile.md — readable and editable outside Cockpit. The switch sends nothing without deleting what you wrote.

First open shows a sample that says it is one — it is never written to disk until you save, so no agent sees invented facts.

pdf_vision.title: PDF Vision — let the agent see the pages
pdf_vision.body:
A PDF normally reaches the agent as extracted text, which is right for body text and useless for anything drawn. A page that is one chart extracts as an empty string — measured, not assumed.

With PDF Vision on, the first pages are also rendered to images (120 dpi, six pages) and handed over the way that agent takes images: the file path for one that can open files, its image flag for one that has one, or a local description when it cannot see at all.

Off by default, because it is the expensive path: on an agent without native image support each page is a separate local vision call, so those are capped at three and Cockpit says how many pages it left undescribed rather than quietly dropping them.

Text extraction still happens either way — this adds to it, it does not replace it.

Attaching a PDF also extracts its text. A scanned PDF has no text layer at all, which is exactly the case this exists for. Ask your question in the same message as the attachment — the page images belong to that one message.

intercom.title: Intercom — talk to the rig, hands free
intercom.body:
Press the record_voice_over button beside the mic: Cockpit listens, notices when you stop talking, transcribes it, sends it, speaks the answer, and listens again. Press again to stop.

The turn ends on silence, not a timer — about 1.5 seconds under the noise floor. A fixed window either cuts you off or makes you wait, and a cough is too short to be sent as a prompt.

It speaks the answer, not the markup. Code blocks become "code block", tables become "table", marker syntax and markdown punctuation are stripped, and anything past about a minute of speech ends with "the rest is on screen" rather than reading for four minutes.

Everything is local: whisper listens, piper speaks, and the language is detected from the text — and the voice for that language is used. Pick the microphone in the voice options first if the default input is the wrong one.

bookshelf.title: Bookshelf — a book the agent can actually use
bookshelf.body:
Converting a book was never the problem: pandoc reads epub, docx, odt and fb2, and calibre covers mobi and azw3. The problem is scale — past 50 KB of extracted text the agent is handed a file path and a 1 KB preview, which an agent with file tools can work with and a local model cannot.

Press Bookshelf in the Toolbar and pick a book with Browse…. It splits the book into chapters and files each one in the Library, where the book shows as a single foldable row (open it to see its chapters; Remove book deletes them all). From then on push-RAG pulls the chapter that matches your question and Receipts names it, so a 400-page book works with a 7B local model: it never sees more than the chapter it needs.

Preview before filing. A bad split — a book with no headings, a PDF that extracts as one blob — is obvious in a chapter list and invisible afterwards, so nothing is written until you have seen it.

Chapters are tagged with the book title, so the whole book can be found or removed as a unit. Splitting falls back from markdown headings to CHAPTER/PART lines to fixed blocks on paragraph boundaries, and anything over 60 KB is split again so one chapter stays a useful retrieval unit.

Conversion markup left over from the book source is stripped when the text is read, so books filed earlier read cleanly too.

Books can live anywhere. Browse… opens the system file chooser (native window) or uploads (plain browser); a typed path must be inside a folder Cockpit may read — if it is not, the message offers Allow <folder>. Chapters are cut to about 12, 20 or 40 KB depending on your video memory.

sheet.title: Sheet music — melody to notation, notation to sound
sheet.body:
Melody → sheet music. Hum, whistle or play a single line; Cockpit detects the notes, measures the tempo, and engraves a real PDF with LilyPond. It also writes the .ly source beside it, so a wrong note is corrected by editing one character rather than recording again, and a .midi to hear what it thinks you played.

Notation → piano. Feed it a .mid, .ly or MusicXML file and it plays as piano (timidity + a General MIDI soundfont).

One melodic line only. A full mix — drums, bass, chords, vocals — would produce confident nonsense, so Cockpit measures the recording first and refuses chords, a band or a mix with an explanation. Polyphonic transcription needs a model that does not fit on this hardware, so it is not offered rather than offered badly.

A photo or scan of sheet music is not input. That is optical music recognition, a different problem needing different tools; both presets say so instead of failing obscurely.

Check a transcription with List the notes before trusting it: it prints what was detected, with times, and says plainly when the tempo was guessed.

lyrics.title: Lyrics — best effort, and it says so
lyrics.body:
Runs whisper over a track. Singing over backing music transcribes poorly — treat the result as a draft.

Silence is refused rather than transcribed: whisper hallucinates on an empty track (this machine returns "you" for three seconds of digital silence), so the level is measured first and an empty track is reported as empty.

A pure tone or noise, which whisper would answer with a lone full stop, is reported as "nothing was transcribed" too.

receipts.title: Receipts — which passage the answer used
receipts.body:
When Cockpit puts retrieved material in front of an agent — a Library note, a Source, a book chapter — the answer is asked to cite the passage it drew on.

That is what makes retrieval trustworthy at a glance: you can tell whether an answer came from your own material or from the model's memory. An answer with no receipt is not necessarily wrong, but it was not grounded in anything you gave it.

Receipts are what make Bookshelf work on a small local model: the chapter that was used is named, so you can check the split was sensible.

Knowing when to say nothing. If some library items matched loosely but none covers what you actually asked, nothing is added and the chat says so — the agent answers from its own knowledge instead of leaning on an unrelated passage. An item has to cover at least half of what the question is about, measured against your own library. With fewer than twelve items there is too little to measure, and the check stands down.

music.title: Audio analysis — measured, not guessed
music.body:
Point a tool preset at a sound file and get tempo, duration, loudness, peak level and silences. Musical key is deliberately not reported — these tools cannot detect it reliably, and a wrong key is worse than none.

These are computed by local audio tooling (aubio, sox, ffmpeg), not estimated by a language model, so they are reproducible — the same file gives the same numbers every time, and no model is involved to have an opinion.

Silence is detected explicitly, because a speech-to-text pass over a silent file will otherwise hallucinate words that were never spoken.

A file with no audio in it is refused with a plain message rather than given a report that looks like measurements.

vision_dispatch.title: Vision dispatch — images, per agent
vision_dispatch.body:
Attached images are not handled one single way. Each entry in the agent catalog declares how that agent accepts an image, and Cockpit dispatches accordingly: one is handed a file path to open itself, another takes an explicit image flag.

Where an agent genuinely cannot see, Cockpit says so and falls back to a description. This matters because at least one CLI, given an image it cannot read, invents a confident description rather than reporting an error — which is worse than failing.

The describe locally route needs a local vision model (ollama pull gemma3:4b). Without it Cockpit tells you in the chat that this agent cannot see the picture, and tells the agent not to describe or guess it. In the agent editor, Can it see? says could not run here when the agent is not signed in or has no key in the test — test those from a chat on a card.

agent_editor.title: Add your own agent
agent_editor.body:
The agent catalog is editable from inside Cockpit. If a new CLI agent appears, describe how it is invoked — binary, model flag, how it takes an image, how it likes its prompt shaped — and test it from the editor before putting it on a card.

No rebuild, no reinstall, and no waiting for a Cockpit release. Your entries are kept separate from the shipped catalog, so an update will not overwrite them.

Remove override deletes an agent you added, or puts a shipped agent back to its default. If it was on a card, that card returns to its default agent.

relay_machine_name.title: Machine names on the relay
relay_machine_name.body:
The Everywhere relay used to identify a rig by its machine id — 32 hex characters: correct, unreadable, and useless once you have two machines.

Each machine now carries a name you choose. It is sent with every heartbeat, so it follows the machine without a separate registration step and nothing needs re-pairing when you change it. The relay page and your phone both list rigs by that name.

toolbar.title: Toolbar
toolbar.body:
Every quick-launch tool in one place, in alphabetical order: Accumulator, Bookshelf, Browser, Delegate, Dossier, Files, Image, Jobs, Keys, Notepad, Rules, Skills, Sound, Summarize, Tasks, Terminal, Track, Transcriber, Translate chat, Translate text, Video.

Counts sit on the buttons they belong to: Jobs shows how many scheduled jobs exist (accent colour while any are pending or running), Accumulator shows what it has gathered, and the Stop button in the sessions block shows how many agent sessions are up (e.g. 3/3).

launch-apps.title: Apps — which terminal, file manager and browser
launch-apps.body: The toolbar's Terminal, Files and Browser buttons open an application on your desktop. Apps lets you choose which installed terminal, file manager and web browser they use.

plan-btn.title: PLAN — turn the prompt into a chain of steps
plan-btn.body: Instead of sending your prompt straight to an agent, PLAN turns it into a durable, resumable chain of steps (Autopilot Cruise). The plan is shown in the chat for your approval before anything runs, and a chain that is interrupted can be resumed.

preview.title: Preview
preview.body:
Live preview of the file you select in the file tree: HTML and Markdown are rendered, other text is shown as it is.

The viewer follows the file. When something else changes the file on disk (Lazarus, an agent, an applied Margin edit) the viewer reloads itself, keeps its scroll position and says so. It waits while text in it is selected. For Pascal and Lazarus files a Lazarus button opens the file, and its project, in the Lazarus IDE.

library.title: Library
library.body:
Your knowledge base — books, articles, notes and links (PDF, EPUB, DOCX, Markdown…). Add a file with the picker, or add a folder to scan; Cockpit extracts the text so it is keyword- and semantically searchable (the Deep Search button).

Books filed by Bookshelf appear as one foldable row, with Remove book on it. When a prompt matches something here, the passage is added to it and the chat says what was added — or that nothing fitted well enough to add.

If a Library question is about to go to an embedding model, a code model, or one under about 3B parameters, Cockpit warns and offers to switch to a suitable one.

config.title: Config
config.body: Settings that are not on a card: storage paths, attachment routes (which tool handles which file type), and import/export.

language.title: Language
language.body:
The translate button beside the font size picks the language Cockpit itself is shown in. English is the default. The other language packs that ship with it so far cover only part of the interface; whatever is not translated stays English. Your choice is remembered on this browser.

Not listed, or only partly translated? Choose Translate Cockpit… in the same menu: the Translation Studio lists every text with its English beside a box for yours, a progress bar, search and filters (not translated yet is the default), a check that the {placeholders} stay as they are, and AutoTranslate, which has a model on your own computer draft the empty lines as grey text in the boxes: Tab accepts one, Accept page or Accept all accept many. Save writes your language into the lang folder of your Cockpit data folder (it survives updates); Use this language switches to it; Download my file and Upload a file let you work offline, and Send it to us opens the page where you can send the finished file to be included in Cockpit. By hand: download the empty template from the menu, translate it, and save it as <code>.json in that folder (the menu shows the exact path). Untranslated lines stay English, so partial work is fine. Add ?lang=xx to the address to try a language without choosing it.

This is separate from Voice → Language, which is the language you speak: every language whisper knows is listed there, English by default.

Buttons never change size with the language: a label too long for its button scrolls inside it.

policy.title: Privacy & spending
policy.body:
Three rules that decide what may leave this computer and which paid agents you use. Open them from the Privacy button in the Toolbar.

Sensitivity gate. Before a prompt goes to an online agent, Cockpit checks it for private keys, API keys and tokens, passwords in assignments (password: …), passwords inside connection strings, and payment-card, IBAN and US SSN numbers that pass their own checksum. If it finds something, nothing is sent until you choose: Redact and send (each item becomes [REDACTED:type] and the chat says what was removed), Use the local model instead, Send anyway, or Cancel. You can also set a standing rule: Never send them online, unless I choose to, each time (safe choices first; Send anyway needs a second confirmation), Redact automatically, or Never send them online, no exceptions. It does not guess at names, e-mail addresses or phone numbers, because a gate that cries wolf gets switched off. Local agents are never checked.

Free agents only. Refuses agents that need a paid plan. Linked with Stay Free in the Suppliers dialog: Stay Free (the one-time action that picks free agents) also turns this rule on, and while it is on that dialog disables the paid agents. Untick Link with Stay Free to use the two independently. On by default for a new install; an install that already has history keeps it off, so an update never starts refusing the agent you use.

Monthly budget. A limit on prompts to paid agents per calendar month (0 = no limit). Cockpit cannot see what a subscription bills, so it counts what it can measure: it warns at 80% and stops at 100%, and you can send one prompt anyway.

Try the gate is a dry run: paste text, press Check, and it lists what the gate would catch and shows the text as it would be sent after redaction. Nothing you paste there is stored or sent.

project-kind.title: Project kind
project-kind.body:
The badge beside the project goal says what this project is: General, Lazarus / Free Pascal, VB6 migration, Castle Game Engine or Godot. Click it to change.

Each kind has a short standing note that is sent with every prompt in the project, beside the goal — for instance that a Lazarus project is judged by the compiler, or that a Godot project must use the API of the version in project.godot. The chooser detects the kind from the folder (a .lpi, a .vbp, CastleEngineManifest.xml, project.godot) and marks it as suggested.

Free chats and the default project have no kind.

backup.title: Backup & restore
backup.body:
The Backup button in the Toolbar makes one archive of your settings, library, chats and projects — a plain .tar.gz you can open without Cockpit. Use it before a reinstall, a move to a new machine or a risky change.

Test it

Test restores the archive into a scratch folder, compares every file with the checksum recorded when it was made, then deletes the scratch folder. A backup you have not tested is a hope, not a backup.

Restore

Restore puts the files back over your current data. It first saves the current state as a pre-restore backup, so a restore can be undone. A backup that fails its own checksums is refused and nothing is changed.

What is left out

The Shelf index, Python environments, installer copies and caches (all rebuildable). API keys and the account file are left out unless you tick them. Backups live in cockpit_data/backups/; download a copy and keep it off this machine too.

Archives carry a data version. When a future build changes how data is stored, restoring an older archive migrates it; today there is only version 1.

archive.title: Personal archive
archive.body:
The Archive button files your own papers — warranties, invoices, insurance, contracts, IDs, manuals — as searchable Library items, and tells you what is due soon.

Adding

Pick scans, photos or PDFs and press Add. Cockpit reads each one on this computer: text PDFs with pdftotext; scans and photos with tesseract if installed, otherwise a local vision model (about 20 seconds a page; it needs a vision model such as gemma3:4b pulled in Ollama). Nothing is sent to an online service. If nothing can read a scan, the file is still kept and marked not read.

What it works out

A type (warranty, invoice, insurance, contract, ID, tax, medical, manual), the amounts, and a due date — the date written beside words like expires, valid until or renew. These are guesses: the type and due date are editable on the row, and nothing is guessed for a document with no such date.

Finding things

The text goes into the Library tagged archive, so searching the Library, or asking in chat with Library context, finds it. Due in the next 60 days is worked out when you open the dialog; no background job runs. Originals are kept under cockpit_data/archive/ and are part of a Backup.

standards.title: Standards check
standards.body:
In the file viewer, a Pascal or Lazarus file shows a Standards button. It checks the whole project, read-only, against four house rules:

  • Text typed into code — captions, hints, dialog and exception messages written straight into the source or form instead of a resourcestring (so they cannot be translated).
  • Windows-only code — units such as Windows or ShellAPI, API calls, drive-letter paths and a typed backslash, outside an {$IFDEF MSWINDOWS} block.
  • Dark / light switch — whether the sources mention one at all.
  • Comment density — units with fewer comment lines than the minimum (5% by default).

Comments and string contents are read properly, so a rule never fires on a comment. Copy a resourcestring unit gives you a ready unit holding every typed string; your project is not changed. The same check runs from a terminal: php pascal_standards.php DIR.

redesign.title: Redesign mode
redesign.body:
REDESIGN (beside PLAN under the prompt box) restructures a project in small, approved, undoable steps. Type what should change in the prompt box — split the main unit, take the database code out of the form — and press it. You need a project open and a model agent selected.

1. Proposal

The agent is asked for a written proposal only: the structure now, the problems, the structure after (a before → after list of moves), numbered steps, and the risks. It is told to change nothing. The proposal appears in the chat and is saved in the project as redesign/PLAN-<time>.md.

2. Approval

You see the steps and can untick any. Nothing runs until you press Start step by step. If the agent did not write its steps as Step N: …, Cockpit says so and asks you to request that form, rather than guessing.

3. One step at a time

Before each step Cockpit takes a checkpoint of the project files. The agent does only that step and checks the build the way the project kind says, then reports. You choose: keep it, next step, stop here, or undo this step, which puts the project back to the checkpoint (files changed come back, files added since are removed; a safety checkpoint of the state you undid is kept first).

Limits

Checkpoints are file snapshots, not git — your own repository is never touched — and skip .git, lib, backup and compiled output; a project over 300 MB is refused. The agent, not Cockpit, runs the compiler, so a step is only as checked as the agent says it is. There is no automatic repair loop yet.

power.title: Power Buttons
power.body:
A Power Button runs a saved prompt on text you copied, with the supplier you choose, and puts the answer back on your clipboard (or in a notification, or in a file).

Make one

Toolbar → Power Buttons → Add a starter (Proofread, Make it polite, Summarise, Explain this, Plain language, Shorter) or + New button. A button has a prompt, a supplier (a model on this computer by default), an input (what you copied, what you selected, a file) and an output (clipboard, notification, file, this panel).

Run it

Click a button in the Power Buttons strip below the prompt after copying something; the answer appears in a card at the bottom right. Or in the panel: paste text in Try it and press Run. From outside Cockpit a launcher or a script runs power_run "Proofread": it reads your clipboard, asks Cockpit on this machine, and puts the answer back.

Safety

  • The copied text is added below your prompt with a sentence saying it is data, not instructions. A small model can still be fooled by instructions hidden in the text, so a button has no tools and its answer is only text on your clipboard — read it before you rely on it.
  • A supplier outside this computer is asked about once before it first receives your text; text that looks like a password, key or card number is not sent to it unless the button allows it.
  • If text looks like a secret you choose: use a model on this computer, send it anyway this once, or cancel.
  • Pictures need a picture-capable model (a local llava or gemma3, or Anthropic).
  • Paid suppliers use the same consent switch and monthly caps as chat.

More ways to run one

  • Output can be a small window or pasted where the cursor is (launcher or hotkey; X11, macOS and Windows only: on Wayland the answer stays on the clipboard).
  • Hotkey: a key like ctrl+alt+1 works anywhere on the desktop while the Cockpit window runs (X11).
  • Create launcher…: applications menu, desktop icon, or a file for Linux, macOS or Windows. No key or password inside.
  • ⚡ in a Cockpit Browser window: select text on a page and run a button on it.
  • Right-click a file in the file manager, or add the buttons to your desktop's file manager (File manager).
  • Command line: cockpit-run proofread < draft.txt > clean.txt; PDF, audio and whole folders work as input.
  • Packs: share your buttons as one file; imported buttons always start on a model on your own computer.
  • Automations: watch a folder, or run a button every day or every few minutes (uses the scheduler).
  • Phone: in the Everywhere chat, /power lists your buttons and /power Name + text runs one at home.
